I bought this during the Summer Sale.
It took me about 3.6 hours to complete this game (including bio breaks where I left the game on) and I got about half of the achievements.

I make it a point to go into games blind. Once I picked up the first season of Orwell, not knowing what to expect was definitely the right way to go.

From the get-go, the mere concept of Orwell was enough to get me hooked. Looking into the lives of people in secret, acting like Big Brother, it's a concept that isn't explored that much in fiction. There's obviously 1984 by George Orwell, which this game references alot in its achievements, but other than that I can't think of anything else.

Orwell's story is definitely the best part. It's thrilling and engaging, with twists coming when you least expect them. After playing it blind, this is even more emphasized. The choices you make can also have a huge impact on the outcome of the story, which adds replayability to the game. It can get emotional at times, though not in the "oh my god, I'm going to cry" kind of way. More like "oh my god, what have I done?" The story can also be considered a kind of social commentary on the world, especially concerning surveillance and data and the repurcussions of them (Snowden, anyone?)

Orwell doesn't have much going for it in terms of gameplay, it's really just clicking and dragging. That would normally be a problem if there wasn't an engaging story to back it up, which I think I've already established Orwell has. There were some points that felt a bit slow, such as the dialogue sections that you can't skip through. That might have improved the pacing just a bit, but it didn't detract from the overall experience too much. It's also a bit short, taking me only around 3 hours to complete my first playthrough, but with the different choices affecting the story, again, this adds to the replayability value.

Basically, just go play Orwell.

Big Brother watches you. That’s what they told us back in the days, when it was just some kinda fiction and a fantastic story. Now, in our present times this issue has become like a real problem, especially for someone who believes, that their lives are important as hell and like to play a private card all the time. 

The government can learn about you literally everything, thanks to social media, your online purchases, all the cameras hanging around the city, watching at you, information you provide to your employers when you attend to job, mobile phones you use with a GPS modules, etc. 

It can be a problem for lots of people, especially for some who is paranoid and doesn’t seem to be busy all the time with any kind of work (because, otherwise, they wouldn’t have time for these kind of thoughts). On the other hand, it can be really helpful to identify a threat and prevent some kind of tragedy from a single murder to a massive terrorist attack.

Orwell try to develop this idea. In this game, which presents as a visual novel with its own dystopia universe, you have to identify the threat. You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life.

So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions.

And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed.

At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. 

Orwell is definitely a blast. It has this unique kind of a gameplay with its deep idea and rich stories for someone, who truly values games as a real art. The combination of twists, turnabouts and all these thrilling moments make this game a great place to spend a few hours, maybe dozens of hours, if you will feel like having more than one run to reveal all the achievements and endings. 

Okay, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:

+ Conspiracy theory lover
+ Love the idea of investigating and matching data and clues into one piece 
+ You want to entertain yourself in a great story game for at least few hours
+ Like to dig to the bottom to find out who is who
+ Fan of dramatic stories with its twists, thrilling moments and surprises

Recommend to avoid if you:

- Don’t get the idea of visual novel
- Not a fan of all these talks that government spy on you and we are all under control.  

Enjoy!

This game is an unexpected little gem.  In case you didn't figure it out, this game is more than just a title reference to the novel 1984.  In it, you play as a government investigator using monitoring tools to spy on people's conversations, web history and personal data in order to find the culprit of certain terrorist attacks and, if possible, prevent any more.  The game is very text-and-pic heavy, so don't expect a graphic adventure where you get to walk around.  All your spying is done from your computer and save from an intro cutscene you don't get to see anything outside your character's monitor.

Don't let that discourage you, though, this game is quite interesting, and smart.  You play by acquiring data from certain media, trying to find people of interest and then use any data you can find on them to expand your knowledge, extrapolate and be able to find even more data, so you can pursue your goal.  For instance, you might a person of interest mentioning a friend over a conversation.  Following that person's name in social media you might find a picture and a nickname, so you can then read comments made with it that establish a possible motivation, which you can then link to certain dates and articles to establish that friend as another person of interest.  Doing more digging, you might be able to find their phone number, so you can read some chats that will give you clues or even a confession that can lead to an arrest.

Yes, there's a whole debate about weighing the pros and cons of a system like this one, where a government has to violate privacy in order to provide security, and there are many works of fiction that tackle the issue, but this one doesn't take the easy way out.  It allows you to play the investigative side and then it lets you choose what to do.  You are the middle man between the information and the government, and as such you can play the loyal dog and do everything as requested, or you can purposely hide information or feed misinformation in order to either exonerate or condemn a person, whether, in either case, that person is innocent or not.

This means that, effectively, the fate of several people is at your hand.  People can (again, innocent or not) be arrested or be free because of your doing.  Your intervention will be pivotal in deciding if a person lives or dies.  Granted, many parts of the game are still linear, and the story progresses at a certain pace, but the game still does a good job of showing that when you get to make a choice, it matters.

These choices give the game enough replay value, and many of them have achievements tied to them if you're a hunter.  I definitely recommend the game.  If you're not sure, you can play the demo, which does a pretty good job of showcasing the gameplay without revealing all of its tricks.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Much less a game than an interactive story. It's a slim game with few objectives and a lot of fluff around it. The game tends to cram exposition into everything, and doesn't allow you to skip or fast-forward any of it. Utimately, while the plot is about making a god of machines, it doesn't justify its deus ex machina storytelling.

[h1]Show, Don't Tell[/h1]
I do not know who's idea it was to not allow the player to fast-forward or skip dialogue, but it was a [b]terrible[/b] decision. The sheer amount of exposition and meaningless chatter in the game is astounding. And this isn't a once or twice occurance, it's a regularly reoccuring situation where key bits of info required to advance the plot sit behind a 4 or 5 minute long unskippable dialogue sequence. And that 10+ minute bit right before the end of the game, who thought that was a good idea? And does the "administrator" need to say something every time I upload a piece of relevant info? It's like having Clippy from MS Word permanently built into the game.

Furthermore, the level of hand-holding is ridiculous. First off, for a game about parsing and collecting information, there's very little you actually have to read. The game essentially takes a big neon highlighter and highlights every single thing that might be of importance. Then, they go ahead and show you exactly where you might've missed a clue or hint. Secondly, the game has these "pivotal" moments where you have to decide which one of multiple conflicting statements is true, except that the system highlights conflicts before you even discover them. It's such a self-defeating mechanism. Imagine if the Sherlock novels had Watson discover a false clue and Sherlock responding "But Watson, that can't be the real clue cause I'm going to find the real clue on page 86!"

And if the story was entralling, and the world-building was coherent, maybe those bad gameplay elements could be overlooked. But they aren't. The plot is cheesy and the writing is lazy. How many times do you plan on having a random character with no background conveniently appear to tie-up some loose ends and then disappear forever? It's honestly kind of amazing how a game where everything you do is character building manages to have some of the most one-dimensional characters I've ever seen.

[h1]Breakdown[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Chapter Select:[/b] Thanks for at least not making me have to replay the whole game to get an achievement.
[/olist]
[b]Cons[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Don't stop users from fast-forwarding text.[/b]
    [*][b]Narrative, not Narrate:[/b] I should be able to tell when I come across an important piece of dialogue. I don't need the game to highlight it a bright color, the music to change to be all dramatic, and Clippy at the top exclaiming, "Wow! That piece of dialogue sure seems important!" *wink* *wink* *nudge* *nudge*
[/olist]
[b]Score[/b]: 2/10

[h1]Orwell... or oh well....[/h1]
I love considering our future and wondering how we might become no more than parts of some evolving socially obedient organism, devoid of personal privacy and with it, control of our own lives...  and our truth. For the greater good as it were. It's pure Orwell which probably explains the title.

For mine though, with some retrospect.... this is less about any "Big Brother" surveillance reference that some might have infered by some of the comments I've seen. I think it's much more than that. It's about our inability to recognise a social evolution far more insidious and far more pervasive to society that we're all an unwitting party too. Ourselves. But then... George didn't say what "Big Brother" really was either.

What gets me with this? Hmmm.... The concept is great. It's a scarey thought, possibly not too far removed from what might already be happening. This game attempts to highlight the manipulation of data, of people and of truth to reach a more palatable "truth". A kind of guaranteed "to the victor go the spoils" by first ensuring we're the victor. 

The premise is sound. The execution seems to be not so good - you ultimately click mostly what you're meant to click, read what you're meant to read and do essentially what you're lead, by the nose, towards. 

But I do wonder here. I found I had my own path I wanted to follow, making assumptions from data and threads I had gathered, some quite... spurious although quite compelling. However, either the game forced decisions I would NOT make given same circumstances or would not even allow me to make them at all. Which was annoyingly disconcerting but oddly enough, might actually be very clever and intentional gameplay. I still can't get a fix on it tbh. 

Perhaps the lesson here is that we don't REALLY want disinterested, independent, non affected 3rd parties from doing surveillance or making any kinds of decisions - even controlled ones - on our behalf do we? Nor would we want those disinterested, independent, non affected 3rd party decisions made to appear like objective reasoning and thus proving there is a need to act against people or states... or truth... Are these actions now to be deemed as not only justified but an social imperative... for the owners of the data, oops, sorry, truth?

It'll never happen. Right? RIGHT?

8.5/10 GG.

In Orwell, Big Brother has arrived. And it's you. You are his online eyes having complete access to all types of communication and data as long as you know what to look for. Your task as investigator is to research bombings which are supposedly organized by an activist group called Thought. To do this, documents, phone calls, chats or target computers have to be analyzed. To do this, you have to drag relevant facts into profiles of your targets to enable acting on them. Certain key criteria have to be met to set the full power of law enforcement into action to protect the regime.

The game is a visual novel with limited influence. The challenge is to find the information needed to proceed. Sometimes, the data is conflicted and you have to take a choice what you enter in the profile. Some non-conflicted information can be left out of the profile as well to protect a target.

Orwell consists of five levels. Towards the end of a level, it's possible to get stuck for a while when the last information needed to trigger an arrest is missing and you don't find it. But I was able to finish it without having to resort to guides or forum posts. The ending was sudden and a bit disappointing when the game finished immediately after dragging a piece of information into a profile. Thought was disbanded, the members arrested and I as the investigator was subjected to an investigation as well. So I replayed the last chapter to get a 'good' ending. Freedom prevailed and Orwell was mothballed.

I really enjoyed the style of the game. Digging for information isn't too difficult but there's an odd satisfaction to completing a profile. I didn't really felt morally compelled to act 'good' or think about what I was doing. Papers, Please or 1979 Revolution: Black Friday were more stimulating in this concern. But the experience was completely entertaining.

What you do in this game is basically read through a linear narrative by dragging "datachunks" from right side of your screen to the left. At no point do you have any clue what the consquences might be this time. So sometimes, the dragging of a chunk leads to an arrest and people getting killed, sometimes nothing happens.

All things considered, Orwell is yet another game where you spend most of the time fighting the user interface. Minimal Design strikes once again.

At times, Orwell gives you a really ham-fisted lecture on the value of privacy that would be too cringy even for an elementary school kid. Point in case: one of the protagonists has a fucking Kafka wallpaper on his desktop and his favourite song is "Die Gedanken sind frei"...
The naivité and carelessness with which the retarded tweeny main cast is using "social" media is appalling. Also, I'm pretty sure that a surveillance state would NOT work the way it does in Orwell. In reality, state surveillance is publicly announced so that every citizen thinks twice before saying anything. You wouldn't just introduce total surveillance without anyone knowing (historic example: the Stasi in the German Democratic Republic)
As Mao said: Execute one - educate hundreds.

Addendum:
After a very rough beginning that almost made me quit, I soldiered through the interface and played to the end. Apparently there are multiple endings, but the game forces you to start from scratch and sit through the whole linear experience two (2!)  more times.
Despite my curiosity, I cannot be arsed to re-read 97.5% of the datachunks I already read in order to see the other two timelines.

Pr0 Tip:
[spoiler]You can 'play' Orwell for free.
Just post something your government doesn't like on X...[/spoiler]

Got this game from a Humble Bundle a while ago and finally decided to try it out. I was a little skeptical at first because I do not always enjoy point and click games, but this game does this genre justice. The "game" is story rich and really makes some choices difficult, which is something not may games today can do. Overall, this is definatley worth a play through and maybe a second if you really enjoy these types of games (multiple different endings).

Pros:
- Starts off slow and steady but slowly increases in scale, making it harder to keep track of everyone andwhat they are doing (very cool and the system really makes you like and hate ceratain characters)
- Very unexpected plot twists
- Simple mechanics, but also very unique and fun
- Music becomes very dramatic sometimes, which adds a sort of rush to playing
- You can access more than just websites (calls, texts, Computers, profiles, etc.)
- DLC and maybe more to come?

Cons:
- Hard to feel encouraged to play again (took me 3 hours to finish first playthrough)
- Can be repetetive to some (very specific genre and could be boring to some)
- Endings are similar in a way. (Wish they were a little more unique)
- DLC was not perfect (some say it was good but reviews are mixed)

Overall, the first playthrough for me was fun and I may revisit this game at a later time (maybe even get the DLC). Maybe wait for a sale on Steam or check Humble Bundle for a sale or bundle. 8/10

Overall, I enjoyed this game, though I will say it's almost more of a visual novel than a game as the gameplay is simple and repetitive (you basically just click and drag things - I didn't mind, but I know it's important to some people). That being said, the story is compelling and the cast of characters is richly developed. There are quite a few plot twists to keep things interesting, though [spoiler]the main one at the end is kind of sudden and out of nowhere (personally, I dislike this as I like to look back with hindsight and see all the clues I missed!).[/spoiler]

If I could describe [i]Orwell[/i] in just two words, it would be "surprisingly smart". By that I mean: this is, obviously, a game about ubiquitous government surveillance, and that's not exactly a new theme. It would have been really easy to slap a "Big Brother BAD" plot on this, make it all about how you're one lone hero fighting the implacable government machine, give it a nice feel-good ending and be done with it. Or go the other way and go full grimdark with the boot stamping on a human face, forever. But [i]Orwell[/i] avoids taking the easy way out, and presents a very human story about how real people might act in a world where such a surveillance system exists. Sure, all the endings you can get (and there's a few) are still much more optimistic than George Orwell would be comfortable with, but hey, if you want [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i], you know where to get it.

The gameplay is a simple affair where, in your role as a government agent, you look through available information (websites, chat transcripts, telephone calls) and collect relevant "data chunks", which in turn unlock more avenues for gathering information... and that's less boring than I'm making it sound, honest. For starters, it's not completely linear: sometimes the data you can collect is contradictory, irrelevant, or just plain wrong when taken out of context, and you have to apply your best judgement as to what goes in -- and the very fact that you're telling the system what to think of people based on the information you select comes back to haunt you in the story. Still, if you're looking for a puzzle game, or something that will challenge you beyond "did I forget to click on something somewhere", this isn't it. You're basically here for the story, but there's enough agency that you don't feel like you might as well have been reading a novel.

[i]Orwell[/i] isn't perfect. I got "stuck" once or twice when the game wanted me to put in some information I had deemed not worth uploading, or that I'd left to come back to later when I had more data -- the interface will track what you have and haven't seen, but not what you've seen but haven't acted upon. At these points (and some others) suspension of disbelief suffers a bit by the way the game artificially fences off information that, logically, should be available at any time. The graphics, while suitably stylized, are a bit [i]too[/i] stylized, especially when things need to animate. The music is fine (with some dramatic touches for when you've uncovered particularly dramatic info), but not remarkable. None of these things are deal breakers, though, and overall [i]Orwell[/i] is well worth its price tag as a solid, interactive story experience with an "It Could Happen Here!" theme that makes it that much more compelling.

[b]”An interactive dystopian detective novel at its best”[/b]
 
[h1]The Good[/h1]
 
Orwell is an electrifying, Orwellian, (surprisingly enough) thriller with exciting twists and turns everywhere you look. The varied choices and the believable medium through which they are presented breathe so much life into the world and its characters. The mechanics, while there aren’t many to play with and master, they are polished and intuitive enough to get the point across in a believable manner. The writing and world building have to carry the game almost entirely and I can gladly say Osmotic Studios has delivered in this regard! Further to add to this, the pacing fits well into a fairly short experience, around 4 hours, which allows for easy and frequent replayability.
The choices you make are integral to the twists and turns you take. The way the choices are handled in Orwell are often left ambiguous with their outcome and effect on the world around you. Even then, every choice you make feels as though it has an impact on the world, no matter how small.
 
[h1]The Bad[/h1]
 
Certain aspects of the game can fell sluggish, such as the tiresome phone call logs and the constant (seemingly) dead ends on web pages. There can be a case made for these moments, however, since they do add to the overall integrity of this fictional world. My only fear is that some players may feel a bit disappointed during these moments that are paced so much slower than the bits in which the player is in direct control.
Another personal gripe with this game is that it’s cast, and plot can feel too expansive given the short time period the game takes place over. Certain events can completely go over the player’s head what with so many people and connections to remember.
 
[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
 
Orwell is an excellent example of compelling and effective storytelling told through the interactive medium of video games. It’s easy to get into and while it may not be the easiest narrative to understand, the writing will keep you engaged constantly. However, at times the story does slow down, and it is easy to get fatigued with the sheer amount of writing in this game.
I think it’s easiest to sum up Orwell as an interactive, dystopian, detective novel at its best. In a game that hinges on the “choices matter” idea, it does well in treating the player like an intelligent and competent participant. You have the ability to make inferences that might not accomplish what you’re trying to do. Also, it is important to note that in a game whose themes are centered around a battling of ideals the player’s choices are remarked upon by all characters and it is easy to let your biases make choices for you. I really do recommend this game to those of you that are itching to fit into the shoes of a detective that is a 3rd party in a war of ideals. Be careful with those choices of yours though, you never know who’s watching.
 
[h1]8/10[/h1]
